title: Moses goes out and sees (Exodus 2:11–15)
hookLine: the prince goes out to his people and sees their burdens

cards: Some people grow up very close to suffering, and never see it. The people who clean their houses, cook their food, build their buildings, are right there, and somehow invisible.
Moses grew up in Pharaoh's palace, with food, clothes, and a princess for a mother. Just outside, his own people were making bricks under the whip. He could have lived his whole life without looking.
The Torah skips his entire childhood in a single verse. Then it says: when Moses had grown up, he went out.

teach.b: Every word counts: "he went out unto his brethren, and looked on their burdens." His brethren: he knows who they are. He's not a tourist.
The midrash takes that word looked seriously. Moses didn't just glance, it says. He saw their loads and wept, and put his own shoulder under the bricks to help, one person at a time.
Then he sees something worse: an Egyptian beating a Hebrew.

teach.h: THIS WAY AND THAT, AND NO ONE.
teach.b: The text slows down: he looked this way and that way, and saw there was no man. And he struck the Egyptian, and hid him in the sand. The Torah doesn't praise it, and doesn't condemn it.
The rabbis read that look in different ways. Some say he looked to be sure no one would see. Others say he looked to see whether anyone else would step in, and there was no one; so he did.
The next day he goes out again and sees two Hebrews fighting each other.

teach.h: WHO MADE THEE A RULER OVER US?
teach.b: He tries to stop them, and one turns on him: "Who made thee a ruler and a judge over us?" Are you going to kill me too? The secret is out.
Pharaoh hears and wants him dead, and Moses runs, all the way to Midian.

teach.h: AT THE WELL, HE STILL SEES.
teach.b: There, sitting by a well, he sees shepherds pushing some young women away from the water, and he stands up and helps them. He can't stop seeing.
That's the first thing the Torah tells about the man who will lead the Exodus, before any miracles.
He went out, and he saw.

how: Jewish teachers often point to this passage as the first sign of Moses' leadership: before God speaks to him, he goes out to his people and sees their suffering.

o: and he saw: truly looking, not glancing past
and he went out: leaving the palace behind
a prophet's vision, seeing God in a dream

games.q: what happened when he went out — tap the pairs.

s: the Torah praises Moses for killing the Egyptian
it neither praises nor condemns. the rabbis read the scene in different ways.
the midrash says Moses helped carry the loads
it says he wept over their burdens and put his shoulder under them.
Moses fled to Midian after Pharaoh heard
Pharaoh wanted him dead, and Moses ran.

games.q: you're Moses, a prince of Egypt. you've gone out to see your people, and you see an Egyptian beating a Hebrew. what does the text say you do first?
o: look this way and that way.
games.why: he looks this way and that way, and sees there is no man. then he strikes the Egyptian. the rabbis still debate what that look meant.

practice: Think of a burden someone near you carries that's easy not to see: someone you pass every day on the way to work, a neighbor who's struggling, people in your own city living a very different life than yours.
Don't solve it, and don't look away either. Just see it, honestly, for a minute.

wordCard.voice: Vayar, Hebrew for and he saw, the verb that runs through this whole story: a prince who leaves the palace, looks at his people's burdens, and can't look away.

orig.note: Hebrew: and he saw. the verb runs through this story and into the next: at the bush, God sees that he turned aside to see.

carryVoice: Your line: he went out and saw. The seeing came before the call. Day eighty, done.
